subject: Polity
topic: High Courts — powers and jurisdiction — mixed tiers
description: Articles 214-231, original/appellate jurisdiction, writs, supervisory power, retirement age

questions.stem: The High Courts in India derive their powers and jurisdiction primarily from which Articles?
questions.explanation: Part VI Chapter V of the Constitution — Articles 214-231 govern High Courts. Art 214 — there shall be an HC for each State. Art 226 — writ jurisdiction of HC. Art 227 — supervisory jurisdiction over subordinate courts. Art 230 — Parliament can extend jurisdiction of HC to UTs. Art 231 — common HC for two or more States. Articles 124-147 govern Supreme Court. Articles 32-35 cover Fundamental Rights and SC's writ jurisdiction.

questions.stem: The retirement age of a High Court judge in India is:
questions.explanation: Article 217(1) — HC judges retire at 62 years (was 60 originally; raised by 15th Amendment, 1963). SC judges retire at 65 (Article 124). Tribunals e.g. NGT chairperson — 70 years; CIC — 65 years. CAG — 65 years. Removal of HC/SC judges identical procedure — Art 124(4): proved misbehaviour or incapacity, supported by 2/3 of present and voting + majority of total membership of each House.

questions.stem: Under Article 226, a High Court can issue writs:

options.option_text: Only against persons within its territorial jurisdiction
To any person, authority or government within its jurisdiction OR where the cause of action arose

questions.explanation: Art 226 has WIDER scope than Art 32 (SC). Two grounds — (i) for ENFORCEMENT of Fundamental Rights AND (ii) for 'any other purpose' (legal rights). Art 226 covers any person, authority, government within HC's territory OR where the cause of action arose, even if the authority is outside the HC's territorial jurisdiction (added by 15th Amendment, 1963). Five writs — habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto. Compare Art 32 — only for FR enforcement, but called the 'soul of the Constitution' by Ambedkar.

questions.stem: The first High Courts in India were established in 1862 in:
questions.explanation: Indian High Courts Act 1861 (passed by British Parliament) → 3 HCs at Calcutta, Bombay, Madras (each established 1862, replacing the older Supreme Courts and Sadar Adalats of those Presidencies). Allahabad HC followed in 1866 (4th oldest). Calcutta HC was inaugurated 2 July 1862 — oldest of the three by a few weeks. After 1947 these became Indian HCs; new ones added (Punjab & Haryana 1966, Delhi 1966, Telangana 2019, Andhra Pradesh 2019, etc.). India currently has 25 HCs.

questions.stem: The Chief Justice of a High Court is appointed by the President in consultation with:

options.option_text: Chief Justice of India and the Governor of the State concerned

questions.explanation: Article 217(1) — President appoints HC judges in consultation with the CJI, the Governor of the State and (for puisne judges) the CJ of the HC. After Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998) the COLLEGIUM SYSTEM emerged: CJI + 2 senior-most SC judges for HC appointments; CJI + 4 senior-most for SC appointments. NJAC (99th Amendment, 2014) was struck down by SC in 2015 (Fourth Judges Case) for violating judicial independence. Memorandum of Procedure (MoP) governs the practical workflow.

questions.stem: The 'supervisory jurisdiction' of a High Court over all subordinate courts and tribunals within its territory is conferred by:
questions.explanation: Article 227 — HC has superintendence over ALL courts and tribunals throughout the territory in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction. Excludes military courts (Art 227(4)). HC can call for returns, prescribe forms, etc. Distinct from Art 226 (writ jurisdiction). Both are unique to HCs and not directly available to SC under same article numbers. SC's writ jurisdiction is Art 32; SC's general supervisory power flows from Art 141 (declared law binds all courts).

questions.stem: Common High Court for two or more States (or for States and a UT) is provided for by:
questions.explanation: Article 231 — Parliament may by law establish a common HC for two or more States or for States and UTs. Examples — Punjab & Haryana HC (Chandigarh, since 1966) serves both states + UT of Chandigarh. Bombay HC's principal seat is Mumbai with benches at Aurangabad, Nagpur, Panaji (also HC for Goa, Daman, Diu, Dadra-Nagar-Haveli). Gauhati HC serves Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram, Arunachal. Telangana HC was created 2019 splitting from AP HC.
